## Simple explanation

A model is the component that applies a learned pattern to an input. It may
classify an image, estimate a number, generate text, or choose an action.

## Technical explanation

In machine learning, a model is often represented as a parameterized function
$f_\theta$ mapping an input $x$ to an output $\hat{y}$. Training selects
parameters $\theta$ using data and an objective. The word can also refer to
the architecture plus learned parameters, or to a serialized artifact used
for inference.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

The model is only one part of an AI system. Preprocessing, postprocessing,
data dependencies, configuration, serving infrastructure, and evaluation
influence the behavior users experience. Clear artifact and version
management helps ensure that the intended model is deployed.

## How it works

A trained model receives input in the format it expects and computes an
output. For example, a neural network performs a sequence of learned
transformations. Its output may be a class score, probability, numeric
estimate, embedding, or generated token.

## Practical example

A trained image classifier takes a preprocessed image and returns scores for
possible classes. Application code can select a class or present the scores
to a user.

## Common misconceptions

- A model is not the entire application or data pipeline around it.
- A model's learned parameters do not explain where its training data came from or what its output means.
- Two files called by the same model name may differ in version, configuration, or preprocessing assumptions.
